https://metro.co.uk/2024/01/13/wore-a-wi.title: My daughter’s six-word reaction to my bald head made me take drastic action
https://metro.co.uk/2024/01/13/wore-a-wi.text:
‘You don’t look like Mum anymore,’ my six-year-old daughter, Georgia, sobbed when she saw my shaved head for the first time.
It was October 2022, and I had been having chemotherapy for around four weeks.
At first, my long brown hair had fallen out in clumps, but in the last week or so my scalp had become itchy and sore. My husband, Chris, was the one to suggest I shave it all off, and reluctantly, I had to admit it was time.
Nothing could have prepared me for Georgia’s reaction, though. It nearly broke me.
I didn’t want to upset her, nor did I want her to see how truly devastated I was at losing my locks.
Instinctively I reached for her pink Trolls wig on the dining table. ‘I don’t have to be bald,’ I said, wiggling the luminous pink wig on my head. ‘I can wear this.’
Gradually a smile appeared beneath her tears and her older brother, Max, found my new ‘do hilarious.
‘Shall I wear it to school tomorrow?’ I joked.
‘Do it, I dare you!’ Max laughed.
The next morning I pulled on the bright pink wig and drove the kids to school in it. There were lots of giggles from both kids and parents and of course, questions too.
I answered as honestly as I could, but mostly I was grateful that this wig was opening a conversation about breast cancer.
I first felt the lump in my left breast four months earlier in June. I’d been lying in bed when I felt a sharp pain, and when I checked where it came from I felt a lump the size of a pea.
At first I didn’t say anything to Chris. I’d found another lump months earlier but my GP had put it down to hormonal changes, so I reasoned this must be the same thing.
But over the weeks, the pain kept coming back. Eventually I confessed what I’d felt to Chris who told me I had to get it checked out.
Expecting it to be nothing more than a routine examination and then be sent on my way, I booked an appointment right before our holiday.
Despite my GP believing it was probably just a cyst, I was given an urgent referral to a breast cancer team.
An ultrasound and a biopsy followed a week later and we were told that if we didn’t hear back, everything was fine. If it was cancerous, they would contact me.
We jetted off to Menorca soon after and though I wanted nothing more than to forget everything and enjoy myself, on the second day of our holiday the hospital called. They wanted me to go back in.
‘It’s bad news then,’ I said to Chris, tears immediately falling. For the rest of the week, I put on a brave face for the kids, but I couldn’t relax.
The day after we landed, we headed to the hospital for my appointment. When the consultant uttered the words: ‘You have triple negative breast cancer (TNBC)’ the room fell quiet.
There was a history of breast cancer on both sides of my family, so I knew it was possible that I was at greater risk.
Now I just wanted to know what came next.
My consultant then explained TNBC was more common in women under 40 and sometimes was linked to a fault or mutation in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene.
He told us they would do a test to see if I had the gene, and that I’d start chemotherapy in the coming weeks.
Two days later, Chris and I sat down with Max and Georgia to break the news.
As I struggled to get the words out, Chris stepped in: ‘Mum’s been diagnosed with breast cancer and needs lots of medicine to make her better.’
‘Is it the same as Nanna’s?’ Max asked. ‘Are you going to die?’
My heart broke. We’d lost my mum to multiple myeloma the year before, a type of cancer that develops from plasma cells in the bone marrow.
‘No, the doctors have caught it early,’ Chris reassured him. ‘They know what they’re doing.’
Being six, Georgia didn’t really understand the situation and innocently asked for a KitKat, effectively ending the discussion there.
I stopped work as a primary school teacher immediately and started weekly chemo in September, before moving onto a stronger version every three weeks.
Exhausted doesn’t even begin to cover how I felt. There were days I couldn’t even stand up, I was sick all the time, constipated, had the worst headaches, and then I started losing my long brown hair.
‘What if I have a really ugly head?’ I said to Chris as he pulled out the clippers and laid down a towel to catch what was left of my locks.
‘There’s only one way to find out,’ he smiled.
Adjusting to my new look wasn’t easy, and upsetting Georgia was never part of the plan. But it did lead me to that pink wig.
Day after day, I would adorn myself with new wigs and headwear for the school drop-off. One day I’d wear a witch’s wig, the next a Halloween hat, a rainbow clown afro or an Ariel wig.
CoppaFeel! offers these simple steps on how to check your own chest for signs of cancer.
Look
Be aware of any changes in size, outline or shape and changes in skin such as puckering or dimpling.
Feel
Be aware of any changes in skin such as puckering or dimpling, or any lumps, bumps or skin thickening which are different from the opposite side.
Notice your nipples
Be aware of any nipple discharge that’s not milky, any bleeding from the nipple, any rash or crusting on or around your nipple area that doesn’t heal easily and any change in the position of your nipple
And though it started off as something to make the kids laugh, I soon had another idea.
‘I could carry this on and raise money for charity,’ I told Chris one night as I rummaged for the next day’s look.
He came up with the name Wig-on-her (a pun for me being a Wiganer) and I also set up a JustGiving page. There I shared photos of the daft wigs and hats I was wearing and soon people were sending me more wigs to wear, along with donations for Breast Cancer Now.
I wore something different every day – everything from a big blue Mohican and a turkey hat to long blonde wigs and a Homer Simpson head. One day I even wore a head-to-toe whoopie cushion outfit which, naturally, got the most laughs.
That was only the beginning. Not long after, the school I had worked for held a ‘crazy head’ day, to raise even more money.
Standing in the playground and seeing all the staff and children wearing silly headgear on my behalf made me well up. Their effort and generosity was overwhelming.
The children had been very creative: some made their hair stand on end, while others looked like they had real cakes in their hair, with fantastic swirling buns. In total, they raised £100.
In January 2023, my chemo came to an end and the following month, I had a single mastectomy to remove my left breast.
I didn’t see the results of the surgery for about a week because of the dressings but when I first took it off, I felt relieved. It didn’t look as bad as I’d built it up in my mind.
With the scar healing, I asked if the kids wanted to see – they were always walking in on me in the bathroom anyway, so this way there’d be no nasty surprises.
When they both agreed, I tentatively removed the dressings to reveal where my left breast used to be. I was worried about how they might react, but I needn’t have.
‘It looks like a smiley face,’ Georgia said and I relaxed, happy she was so unbothered about it.
In April, I started my 15 sessions of radiotherapy but by July – and on my birthday, no less – we received the most amazing news. I was in remission.
When we collected the kids from school, I told them we had something to celebrate. ‘My cancer is gone. No more medicine, I’m fixed.’ I announced.
Max was so happy, and Georgia gave me the biggest squeeze.
But just because this part of my journey was over, it didn’t mean we were done raising awareness.
Later that month we took part in a 5k Family Wig Walk we’d organised earlier in the year.
Seeing 100 people in a sea of multicoloured wigs and hats was just incredible. There was a real buzz among the colourful crowd and to have so many people turn up to support me and the charity was amazing. We raised £2,400 from that one walk alone.
To date we’ve raised over £11,000 for Breast Cancer Now.
As for me, life is starting to get back to some semblance of normal. I’m back at work two days a week but I still have to monitor my health closely.
Triple negative breast cancer is more likely than other forms to recur, so I’m having a yearly mammogram on my right breast and keeping a keen eye out for changes in my body, too.
